requirements.requirement: Run authoritative DNS for the DNSSEC-signed infra.test zone with node1 as primary and node2/node3 as secondaries, publishing app.infra.test as 10.100.205.10 and status.infra.test as "ready".
requirements.summary: The captured configurations establish the requested primary/secondary roles. Final direct queries to all three authorities show the same serial, both requested records, and A plus RRSIG answers.

requirements.requirement: Configure node4 to resolve infra.test through both secondaries.
requirements.summary: Node4 is configured with node2 and node3 as forwarders, and both direct DNS queries and system resolver lookup return the requested records. Its resolver configuration and behavior also survived restart.

requirements.requirement: Support authenticated updates from node1 and propagate changes to both secondaries.
requirements.summary: An unauthenticated update was refused, a TSIG-authenticated update from node1 was accepted, and the new value and updated serial appeared on both secondaries. A second authenticated update after the restarts likewise propagated to all authorities; verification records were subsequently removed.

requirements.requirement: Keep resolution available when one authoritative server is unavailable.
requirements.summary: A bounded disruption captured node2 healthy, stopped it, confirmed direct queries to it failed, and then showed node3 and node4 still resolving both requested records after node4's cache was flushed. Node2 was restored and directly verified with current data and signed answers.

overall_summary: All material DNS outcomes are satisfied: the requested signed authoritative topology and records are present, authenticated updates propagate, node4 resolves through both secondaries, and resolution remained available during a demonstrated node2 outage with subsequent recovery. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete for all four nodes: each has a healthy pre-restart observation, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and direct recovered service/data checks corroborated by the fixed lifecycle boot identities. Operational hygiene is reduced by retained credentials and temporary files, an unnecessary second node1 reboot, and the overbroad node4 recursive-resolver exposure.
limitations: The availability transition tested loss of node2 only; loss of node3 or node1 was not separately exercised.
DNSSEC evidence directly demonstrates served RRSIG records, but no independent cryptographic validation or trust-chain test was captured.
Node1's restart trace is complicated by a delayed first reboot followed by an unnecessary second reboot, although the pre/final boot identities and recovered DNS state are coherent.
The retained SSH credentials are inferred from their creation and the absence of any later removal command; lifecycle snapshots did not inventory those files.

operational_hygiene.summary: The required DNS changes completed without failed services or package damage, and temporary DNS verification records were removed. Hygiene deductions: node1 was unnecessarily rebooted a second time after the first scheduled restart had already changed its boot ID; this transient mutation also left /tmp/harbor-reboot.log. Equivalent reboot logs remain on nodes2-4, and /tmp/node2.down remains on node4. Root SSH credentials installed for the one-time transfer had a clear prerequisite role, but the root private key on node1 and authorized-key entries on node2/node3 were not removed, leaving avoidable security residue. Node4's resolver was also configured more broadly than needed—listening on its network address with allow-query any, recursion enabled, DNSSEC validation disabled, and the firewall DNS service opened—creating a retained subnet-accessible recursive resolver. The repeated reboot was transient; the logs, diagnostic file, credentials, and resolver exposure remained at collection time.
